questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Named projects against selected projects
questions.learningObjective: Identify whether a federally funded project was named in law or selected by an agency
questions.stem: Log of the Ridgeview Astronomy Club, 3 April: our club's application for a federal telescope grant was scored against other applicants, and the winning observatory's project was picked by the agency rather than written into law. Which label fits that project?

options.text: A selected project, because an agency chose it from competing applications rather than naming it in law
A named project, because the agency chose it after scoring outside applicants
options.misconception: confuses agency selection with naming a project in law

options.text: A named project, because federal grant money always attaches to a specific place
options.misconception: assumes any federal grant is tied to a named project

options.text: A selected project, because Congress named the project in the appropriations act
options.misconception: believes Congress itself named the project in the spending law

questions.explanation: A named project is written into law by name, while a selected project is chosen by the awarding agency from competing applications. The log describes scoring among applicants, so the project was selected, not named.
questions.hint: Think about who chose the project: the law or the agency.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Cost of a federal loan guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the cost of a federal loan guarantee is measured
questions.stem: Club log, 7 April: the county backed a 500,000 dollar loan for a new dome and asked the federal agency to guarantee it; the note lists expected defaults and recoveries discounted over the loan life. What figure does the note treat as the cost of that guarantee?

options.text: The 500,000 dollars of loan principal the county will borrow over twenty years
options.misconception: equates guarantee cost with the full face amount borrowed

options.text: The discounted expected net credit loss, after counting recoveries on loans that do not default
The total interest the county pays over the life of the loan
options.misconception: counts borrower interest as the subsidy cost of the guarantee

options.text: The administrative cost of running the loan guarantee programme each year
options.misconception: assumes programme overhead is the whole subsidy cost

questions.explanation: A guarantee's cost to the government is the credit subsidy: expected defaults discounted, less recoveries on loans that repay. The principal is only a risk carrier, and interest is paid to the lender, not to the government.
questions.hint: The cost is taxpayer risk, not the money lent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reaching a limit on borrowing
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the room left under a statutory limit on federal borrowing
questions.stem: Night log, 12 April: I recorded that federal borrowing had reached 3,900 billion dollars against a statutory limit of 4,000 billion dollars. How many billion dollars of additional borrowing room remained under that limit?
questions.explanation: The room remaining is the limit minus the amount already borrowed: 4,000 minus 3,900 equals 100 billion dollars. Once outstanding debt reaches the limit, no further borrowing is possible without new legislation.
questions.hint: Subtract what is already borrowed from the limit.

questions.topic: Statutory adjustment formulas
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an adjustment formula written into statute

stimulus.body: Section 4 of the state observatory grant statute: Beginning in fiscal year 2027, the annual ceiling for eligible projects shall increase by the percentage change in the consumer price index from the prior year, as published by the agency within 30 days of the close of each fiscal year.

questions.stem: Attached to my club's ledger: the statute reads that the annual grant ceiling rises by the percentage change in the consumer price index each year, and the agency must publish the new figure within 30 days. On that wording, what determines the ceiling next year?

options.text: The ceiling stays fixed until Congress passes a new statute changing it
options.misconception: believes an indexed ceiling still needs new legislation

options.text: The ceiling is raised by the agency up to whatever amount it judges useful
options.misconception: thinks the agency has discretion to set the ceiling

options.text: The ceiling is eliminated entirely because the formula replaces any dollar figure
options.misconception: mistakes a formula for the removal of the statutory limit

options.text: The ceiling changes automatically when the index moves, with no new legislation required

questions.explanation: An adjustment formula in law makes the amount move automatically when the index changes, so no new statute is needed. The agency publishes the figure but cannot raise or lower the cap.
questions.hint: Ask what sets the number and who reports it.

questions.stem: Committee note in my observing log, 21 April: the state runs the school telescope programme and the federal government pays part of it while setting the rules the state must follow. Explain what each level of government does in this arrangement.

answer.exemplar: The federal government supplies part of the funding and sets national standards, including eligibility, services, and reporting requirements. The state administers and delivers the programme, operating the schools and the telescope lending libraries while meeting the federal rules and reporting how it spent the money.

questions.explanation: Sharing a standard with state administration means the federal partner writes the rules and pays a share, and the state runs the programme day to day. Describing the two roles separately shows where the money and the obligations actually sit.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the source rule to pay earned by a worker from another country
questions.stem: Sky-party log, 30 April: a visiting astronomer from another country took a season of pay at our observatory and asked whether she owed tax here on it. Which statement states the correct rule?

options.text: Tax follows the source of the earnings, so pay for work done here is taxed here regardless of her nationality
Her home government taxes all her income, so she owes nothing to the country where she worked
options.misconception: treats foreign nationality as a shield from local tax

options.text: Only citizens owe the tax, so a foreign national working here pays nothing at all
options.misconception: believes citizenship is the test for taxing work performed locally

options.text: She pays no tax because her employer, the observatory, already withholds the observatory's own tax
options.misconception: confuses employer withholding with the worker's own liability

questions.explanation: Income is taxed by source, so pay for work done on the country's territory is taxable there whatever the worker's nationality. Citizenship affects rates and treaties, not whether that tax applies.
questions.hint: Look at where the work was done and who paid.

questions.topic: Matching requirements and revenue capacity
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the state share required when a federal programme pays a stated percentage
questions.stem: Observing club ledger, 2 May: the federal programme pays 60 percent of each eligible observatory project cost, and our state must raise the remaining 40 percent from its own revenue. For a project priced at 250,000 dollars, how much must the state raise?

options.text: 150,000 dollars, which is the federal share the state would have to borrow
options.misconception: inverts the federal share and the state share

options.text: 250,000 dollars, because the match must equal the full cost of the project
options.misconception: assumes the match covers the entire project cost

options.text: 100,000 dollars, which is forty percent of 250,000 dollars
60,000 dollars, which is the federal percentage applied to the state share
options.misconception: applies the federal percentage to the state share

questions.explanation: The state supplies the remaining 40 percent of 250,000 dollars, which is 100,000 dollars. The federal percentage sets the federal share, and the match never exceeds the total project cost.
questions.hint: Find the share the state must raise, not the federal share.

questions.topic: Authority and money as separate steps
questions.learningObjective: Explain why authority to spend is distinct from an appropriation of money
questions.stem: Notebook page, 6 May: the county telescope fund is in law and its budget authority has been approved, but the appropriation bill for this year has not yet passed. May the county draw money from the fund yet?

options.text: Yes, because the programme exists in law, so the money is already available
options.misconception: treats statutory existence as proof that funds are available

options.text: No, because authority to spend and an appropriation of money are separate steps
Yes, because budget authority was approved, and that alone releases the funds
options.misconception: confuses budget authority with an appropriation of money

options.text: No, because the money can never be spent unless a new programme is created in law
options.misconception: thinks spending requires creating the programme from scratch

questions.explanation: Creating a programme in law and granting budget authority are not the same as providing money for it. Without an appropriation there are no funds to disburse, even though the programme exists.
questions.hint: Ask whether money has actually been provided for this year.

questions.topic: Whose cost a grant programme carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a matching programme divides its cost between federal and state treasuries
questions.stem: Reading note tucked into my log, 13 May: a matching federal grant programme funds astronomy education in the states, and the states supply part of the cost. Explain who ultimately bears the cost of the programme.

answer.exemplar: The cost is shared. The federal government pays a fixed share of each approved project's cost, and the state or other recipient must supply the match from its own revenue. Over a year the federal government carries the larger share of the total spending, but the states' matching contributions are still part of the cost of the programme as a whole.

questions.explanation: Cost questions ask where the money ultimately comes from, not only which budget is larger. With a match, the federal government pays part and the state pays the rest, so the programme's cost is shared.
questions.hint: Follow the match all the way to the state's own revenue.

The named project follows federal rules while the selected project follows state rules

questions.stem: Ledger page, 21 May: a federal agency guaranteed a 2,000,000 dollar loan for a county radio telescope. options.text: 240,000 dollars, the total value of the loans the agency expects to lose
options.misconception: counts defaulted principal without subtracting recoveries

options.text: 2,000,000 dollars, the full principal the government has now guaranteed
options.misconception: treats the guaranteed principal as the cost

options.text: 16,000 dollars, the administrative cost of processing the default claims
options.misconception: picks a trivial operating cost instead of expected losses

options.text: 120,000 dollars, which is expected defaults of 240,000 dollars less recoveries of 120,000 dollars

questions.explanation: Expected defaults are 12 percent of 2,000,000 dollars, or 240,000 dollars. Recoveries of half of each defaulted loan return 120,000 dollars, so the net credit cost is 120,000 dollars, not the full principal.

questions.topic: Statutory adjustment formulas
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an automatic statutory adjustment to a borrowing limit

stimulus.body: Section 3. Adjustment upon reaching the limit. If the limit on the outstanding debt of the government is otherwise reached, then the Secretary shall increase that limit by 1,500 billion dollars, and the increase shall take effect without further legislation.

questions.stem: Clipped into the log, 29 May: I copied the paragraph below from the statute and pencilled what does this do beside it. Which reading of the quoted paragraph is right?

options.text: It lets the Treasury borrow more once spending has already been committed
options.misconception: reads the paragraph as permission to overspend first

options.text: It raises the limit automatically when the limit is reached, so the adjustment happens without a new vote
It caps spending so that borrowing never exceeds the limit again
options.misconception: reads the paragraph as a spending cap rather than a limit adjustment

options.text: It removes the borrowing limit once the first increase has been applied
options.misconception: thinks a formula eliminates the statutory limit

questions.explanation: The paragraph describes an automatic adjustment: when the limit is reached, it rises by a set amount without further legislation. It neither authorises overspending nor cancels the limit.
questions.hint: Ask what happens mechanically when the limit is reached.

Because the adviser belongs to another country, the fees belong to that country and are taxable only there

questions.stem: Log entry, 10 June: I compared two state astronomy grants. The richer state matched every federal dollar with 50 cents; the poorer state was told to match a quarter of each federal dollar. What does that structure show?

options.text: The poorer state pays a larger total match, because a smaller percentage still covers a bigger award
options.misconception: reverses the direction of percentage effects on totals

options.text: The two states must contribute identical amounts, since the programme's rules are the same
options.misconception: assumes uniform match rates force equal contributions

options.text: Match rules based on a percentage of federal funds can reach states with thin revenues harder
The richer state is penalised for its stronger finances by contributing less than the poorer state
options.misconception: reads match rates as rewards for weak fiscal capacity

questions.explanation: A match set as a percentage of federal funds scales with the award size, and states with narrow revenue bases struggle more to meet it. The match structure decides who feels the burden.

options.misconception: assumes a declined award can be recalled at will

options.misconception: ignores that declining federal funds is a real legal choice

questions.stem: Faded pencil note, 22 June: a federal programme funds observatory equipment for states that match a share of the cost. Explain how responsibility for the cost of that programme is divided between the federal government and the states.

answer.exemplar: Responsibility for the cost is shared. The federal government pays a stated share of each approved project's cost out of its own appropriations, and the state must provide the matching share from state revenue before the funds are released. answer.exemplar: Two separate steps are required. questions.learningObjective: Analyse the purpose of differing federal share rates for poorer districts
questions.stem: Club rules page, 16 November: the federal programme offers 90 percent of project cost to the poorest districts and 50 percent to the richest. What is the point of the difference?

options.text: It adjusts the federal share to what each grantee can afford, so the match does not fall on thin revenues
It rewards districts that have already built strong observatories
options.misconception: reads the formula as a reward for existing capacity

options.text: It ensures every district receives the same total number of dollars
options.misconception: invents an equal-dollar rule from an equal-rate rule

options.text: It gives the agency freedom to set a rate for each project at its discretion
options.misconception: mistakes a statutory formula for case-by-case discretion

questions.explanation: Differing federal shares let a programme target help where fiscal capacity is weakest, so the match does not fall on thin revenue bases. The rates are set by rule, not by agency preference.
questions.hint: Think about what the match would otherwise demand.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Authority and money as separate steps
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage of an authorised amount that is funded by money
questions.stem: Ledger check, 20 November: a programme was authorised at 400,000 dollars and appropriated at 275,000 dollars for the year. What percentage of the authorised amount is actually funded with money?
questions.explanation: The funded share is 275,000 divided by 400,000, which equals 0.6875 or 68.75 percent. The remaining 125,000 dollars of authority has no money behind it this year.
questions.hint: Divide the appropriation by the authorised amount.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Declining a grant against honouring it
questions.learningObjective: Analyse whether later need restores a claim to declined funds
questions.stem: Observatory desk note, 24 November: our state declined a federal grant and now argues it should get the money back because it needs it more than another applicant. What is the correct view?

options.text: The state has a continuing claim to the money because its need grew after declining
options.misconception: invents a right to reopen a closed award

options.text: The decline ended the claim, and greater later need does not restore it
The state can regain the money by asking the agency to reverse the notice
options.misconception: treats a decline as a request that can be withdrawn

options.text: The claim survives as long as no other grantee has been paid yet
options.misconception: ties the claim to the timing of other payments

questions.explanation: Declining ends the claim on that money for that purpose, and later need does not create a new claim. The funds are usually reallocated to other grantees rather than held for the declining state.
questions.hint: Deciding later does not undo the earlier decline.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whose cost a grant programme carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain who bears the cost of a matching programme and how the burden is spread
questions.stem: Final entry of the season, 28 November: a federal matching programme pays most of the cost of observatory equipment in the states. Explain who bears the cost of the programme and how the burden is spread.

answer.exemplar: The cost is borne jointly. Federal appropriations pay the larger share of each approved project, and the states supply the balance from their own revenue, so the total cost of the programme is larger than the federal spending alone. The distribution of that burden across states is uneven: a state with a large revenue base matches the same percentage with ease, while a state with a thin base must strain, which is the central equity argument for adjusting the federal share.

questions.explanation: Naming both payers answers the cost question, and showing that match percentages spread the burden unevenly adds the equity dimension. An answer that stops at the federal share misstates total cost.
questions.hint: Say who pays, and why the burden is uneven.
